implementation_notes: The with statement makes release structural: threading.Lock, RLock and Semaphore implement __enter__/__exit__, and CPython's documentation recommends the context-manager form over manual acquire()/release() whenever practical. Custom scopes - a lock registry, an idempotency or retry guard - are three lines with contextlib.contextmanager, and the same shape covers database sessions (SQLAlchemy's engine.begin()). Explicit acquire/release survives only when the lock's lifetime must span functions or when acquire(blocking=False)/timeout semantics are needed.
pitfalls: The lock is held until the block exits, so an await or a blocking network call inside with lock: holds it for that whole time and, in asyncio code, blocks the event loop.
The GIL does not make read-modify-write atomic; a critical section that re-enters user code which acquires the same lock needs RLock, and a non-reentrant Lock deadlocks on nested with.
threading locks do not cross process boundaries: multiple workers need file locks or the database's own locking instead.

variants.name: framework transaction boundary (Django ATOMIC_REQUESTS / atomic, ORM session)
variants.idiom_name: ATOMIC_REQUESTS = True / with transaction.atomic(): / with engine.begin() as conn:
variants.implementation_notes: The offline variant: with ATOMIC_REQUESTS Django wraps every request in a transaction, so the boundary - and with it the row locks and version checks the ORM issues - is started and finished by the framework rather than by views, and service code contains no begin or commit. Finer boundaries stay declarative with transaction.atomic() as a decorator or context manager (or SQLAlchemy 2.0's engine.begin()), and select_for_update() is the escape hatch when a row must be locked earlier than the first write. Hand-managed commit/rollback per view is justified only for non-ORM, long-running management work.
pitfalls: ATOMIC_REQUESTS keeps the transaction open for the whole request including template rendering, so slow responses hold database locks and code outside the ORM can join the transaction accidentally.
select_for_update() raises TransactionManagementError outside a transaction and holds its lock until the transaction ends, not until the statement ends.
An exception caught inside an atomic block marks the transaction for rollback: further ORM work raises TransactionManagementError unless a nested atomic block provides a savepoint.
